hints: Count the longest continuous carbon chain in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and identify which carbon carries the bromine atom.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain and the substituent position**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. You have four carbons in a row, so the parent is butane. Number from the end that gives the Br the lowest number. The Br is on carbon 2, so the name is 2-bromobutane.

hints: Look at the alcohol $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and decide if the $\text{OH}$ carbon is attached to one, two or three other carbons.
walkthrough:
Link alcohol type to oxidation product**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ the $\text{C-OH}$ carbon is joined to two other carbons, so it is a secondary alcohol. Warm acidified dichromate oxidises a secondary alcohol to a compound with $\text{C=O}$ in the middle of the chain. That class is a ketone, here butan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Keep the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ fixed and think of all the different carbon skeletons for four carbons, straight chain and branched.
Now move the Br to every unique position, remembering that A itself is the 2-bromo straight chain isomer so you need the other three.
walkthrough:
Keep the straight chain but change the Br position**
A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The other straight chain isomer puts Br at the end: $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is 1-bromobutane, a primary bromoalkane.

Branch the chain to make two more skeletons**
With four carbons you can also have a three carbon chain with a methyl branch. Put Br on the branched central carbon to get $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$, a tertiary isomer. Put Br on the end of the branched chain to get $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}$, a primary branched isomer.

hints: Think about what type of reaction replaces Br by OH in reaction 1, and what type of reagent $\text{OH}^-$ is.
walkthrough:
Decode the letters**
Br is replaced by $\text{OH}$, so a substituent is swapped, that is substitution. The attacking species $\text{OH}^-$ is electron rich and attracted to a positive carbon centre, that is a nucleophile. So S stands for substitution and N stands for nucleophilic.
Final answer: S = substitution ; N = nucleophilic

hints: Recall that $S_N1$ starts with the slow loss of the leaving group alone to form a positive carbon intermediate.
Think about why the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks toward Br, using electronegativity to place partial charges.
Consider how the $\text{OH}^-$ ion uses its nonbonding electrons to form the new $\text{C-O}$ bond in the second step.
walkthrough:
Break the polar C-Br bond first**
Br is more electronegative than C, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{-Br}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow starting on the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and pointing to Br. The pair of electrons goes fully to Br to give $\text{Br}^-$, leaving a planar carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. This slow ionisation is the rate determining step.

Show the carbocation intermediate clearly**
Draw the central C with only three bonds, to $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and a full positive charge on C. No arrow is needed from elsewhere in this step, the bond has already broken.

Attack by hydroxide**
Draw $\text{OH}^-$ with its lone pairs and negative charge. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on O directly to the positively charged C. The lone pair forms the new $\text{C-O}$ bond to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{\delta+}\text{-Br}^{\delta-} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}^-$ with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br.
Step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ to carbocation C.

hints: Identify which bond must break in the slow step of the $S_N1$ mechanism for each halogenoalkane.
Recall how bond strength changes down Group 17 as atoms get larger and overlap gets poorer.
Link a stronger bond to a higher activation energy and a slower rate, and a weaker bond to a faster rate.
walkthrough:
Focus on the bond that controls the rate**
In $S_N1$ the slow step is breaking $\text{C-X}$ to form the carbocation. The same carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ forms in all three cases, so the only difference is how easily $\text{C-Cl}$, $\text{C-Br}$ or $\text{C-I}$ breaks.

Compare C-Cl with C-Br**
$\text{C-Cl}$ is shorter and stronger than $\text{C-Br}$, about 340 compared with about 280 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. More energy is needed to break it, so ionisation is slower and the chloroalkane reacts slower than the bromoalkane.

Compare C-I with C-Br**
$\text{C-I}$ is longer and weaker than $\text{C-Br}$, about 240 compared with about 280 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Less energy is needed to break it, so ionisation is faster and the iodoalkane reacts faster than the bromoalkane.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ reacts slower than $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ because $\text{C-Cl}$ is stronger than $\text{C-Br}$.
$\text{CH}_3\text{CHICH}_2\text{CH}_3$ reacts faster than $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ because $\text{C-I}$ is weaker than $\text{C-Br}$.
Bond enthalpies: $\text{C-Cl}$ about 340, $\text{C-Br}$ about 280, $\text{C-I}$ about 240 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

hints: Compare the products: reaction 1 gives an alcohol by substitution, reaction 2 gives $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ by loss of HBr.
Recall the standard solvent and temperature choice that favours elimination of a halogenoalkane over substitution.
walkthrough:
Choose the solvent that favours elimination**
Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ provides plenty of $\text{OH}^-$ as a nucleophile for substitution to the alcohol. Dissolving $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol instead makes $\text{OH}^-$ act mainly as a base, removing $\text{H}^+$ and causing loss of HBr to form the alkene $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$.

Raise the temperature**
Elimination is favoured by hot conditions. Heat the mixture under reflux so the vapour condenses and returns, allowing strong heating without loss, which pushes reaction 2 rather than reaction 1.

Final answer: Use ethanolic (alcoholic) NaOH instead of aqueous NaOH.
Heat under reflux / use higher temperature.
